Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Current imaging shows a partial response but the exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the remaining liver lesions are not provided.  
- No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, vascular or biliary involvement, or liver functional reserve.  
- Because these decisive pieces of information are missing, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The prerequisite action is a detailed volumetric and anatomical reassessment (including FLR calculation and vascular mapping) after further systemic therapy to determine whether an R0 resection with adequate FLR is feasible.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI) for another 2–3 months, adding a biologic agent if molecular profile permits (anti‑EGFR for RAS‑wild‑type, anti‑VEGF otherwise).  
- Perform restaging with contrast‑enhanced MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) and triphasic CT of chest/abdomen to:  
  • Quantify residual liver lesions (size, number, segmental location).  
  • Assess relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
  • Calculate FLR volume; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % with chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
- Evaluate the primary rectal tumor: if asymptomatic, defer definitive rectal surgery until after hepatic clearance (liver‑first approach). If symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction), treat with short‑course radiotherapy and/or surgical resection before liver surgery.  
- Once imaging confirms that all viable metastases can be removed with negative margins while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection:  
  • Aim for an R0 anatomical or non‑anatomical resection of each lesion; combine with intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult disease.  
  • For lesions in locations that would compromise FLR, consider adjunctive local therapies (RFA, SBRT) to achieve complete clearance.  
- Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOXIRI ± targeted agent) and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental location of residual liver metastases after chemotherapy.  
- Relationship of lesions to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted therapy.  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (local stage, symptoms, response to any neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Trend of tumor markers (CEA) after systemic therapy.  
- Tolerance and cumulative dose of prior chemotherapy (risk of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations address key domains including resectability assessment, preoperative imaging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy/surveillance. They both emphasize the need for detailed imaging and restaging, specific surgical strategies, and postoperative management, therefore aligning on completeness.

Step Concordance: Both recommendations classify the case as 'potentially resectable' and require further imaging and assessment to determine resectability. They propose continuing systemic therapy, detailed imaging for restaging, and surgical strategies if R0 resection is deemed possible. Thus, they are concordant in key clinical reasoning steps.

Case Tailoring: Recommendation 1 includes a specific plan for the primary rectal tumor, depending on symptoms, which is not detailed in Recommendation 2. Additionally, Recommendation 1 provides specific systemic therapy regimens based on molecular profiling, while Recommendation 2 suggests a minimally invasive approach and includes liquid biopsies, indicating some differences in case-specific tailoring.

Missing Data Concordance: Both recommendations identify the need for detailed anatomical mapping of liver lesions, future liver remnant calculations, and the molecular profile of the tumor as critical missing information. They both note the importance of the status of the primary rectal tumor and response to therapy, showing alignment in this aspect.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The post‑chemotherapy MRI shows three residual metastases each <2 cm, which from a technical standpoint can often be removed with negative margins while preserving adequate liver parenchyma. However, decisive information required to confirm feasibility – namely quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume (or FLR/body‑weight ratio), precise segmental location of the three lesions, and confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease – is not provided. Because these data are essential to determine whether a curative hepatectomy can be performed safely, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of that assessment (or a prerequisite intervention such as portal vein embolisation if FLR is insufficient).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy to complete an optimal pre‑operative course (typically 6–8 cycles total of a doublet ± anti‑EGFR given RAS‑wild‑type). This consolidates response and provides further “proof of time” for disease biology.  
• Perform a dedicated hepatic work‑up: high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast plus volumetric analysis to calculate FLR; repeat chest CT/PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease; intra‑operative ultrasound planning.  
• If FLR ≥30 % of total liver volume (or ≥0.5 % of body weight) and vascular inflow/outflow can be preserved, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection:  
    – Choose the most parenchyma‑sparing approach (segmental or non‑anatomic resections) to achieve R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
    – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and detect any occult metastases.  
• If FLR is inadequate, employ conversion strategies before definitive resection:  
    – Portal vein embolisation (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the future remnant;  
    – Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or combined resection‑ablation (thermal ablation or SBRT) for lesions in difficult locations.  
• Address the primary rectal tumor after hepatic surgery (or concurrently if technically feasible):  
    – If the rectal primary is locally advanced, give neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by total mesorectal excision;  
    – If already resected or low‑risk, proceed with standard surgical resection.  
• Post‑operative systemic therapy: resume/adjuvant chemotherapy to complete ≥6 months total exposure, incorporating anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status, unless contraindicated.  
• Enrol the patient in a structured surveillance program (CEA, cross‑sectional imaging every 3–6 months) to detect early recurrence.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (or FLR/body‑weight ratio).  
• Exact segmental location of the three residual lesions and their relationship to major vascular/biliary structures.  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes).  
• Performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function tests.  
• Current status and staging of the primary rectal tumor (resected, locally advanced, need for radiotherapy).  
• Details of the chemotherapy regimen used (agents, use of biologics) and RECIST‑based radiologic response.  
These items are essential to finalize resectability and to tailor the definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations cover resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. While they use different terms and slightly different approaches, the major domains are covered, allowing for a completeness score of 1.

Step-by-step concordance: The two recommendations differ significantly in the classification of resectability and subsequent management steps. Recommendation 1 identifies the case as potentially resectable pending further data, whereas Recommendation 2 considers it resectable, pending reassessment. Their management plans differ in terms of step sequence and specific strategies (e.g., treatment of "disappeared metastases"), resulting in a step concordance score of 0.

Case-tailoring concordance: Each recommendation includes different case-specific factors, such as molecular profile implications and specific surveillance targets. Recommendation 2 emphasizes the importance of detailed mapping of all initial metastatic sites and the primary tumor's molecular status, which is less emphasized in Recommendation 1, leading to a case-tailoring score of 0.

Missing data concordance: The types of missing information identified in both recommendations overlap but are not identical. Recommendation 1 focuses on FLR, vascular/biliary relationships, and performance status, while Recommendation 2 emphasizes the mapping of disappeared metastases and molecular characterization of the primary tumor. The lack of alignment in identified essential data results in a missing data concordance score of 0.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 Rationale:  
  – After systemic therapy the patient still has 7 viable liver metastases, including one lesion (segment VII, 5 cm) that is progressing despite chemotherapy, indicating active disease biology.  
  – Current guidelines state that “significant progression of metastatic disease (growth in more than three existing liver metastases and/or development of new lesions) during optimal pre‑operative chemotherapy” should prompt further systemic or regional therapy before attempting resection.  
  – Technical resectability cannot be confirmed without data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, vascular involvement, and the bilateral distribution of the remaining lesions.  
  – Therefore a prerequisite action – attainment of disease control of the progressing lesion (e.g., change of systemic regimen and/or local ablative therapy) and confirmation of adequate FLR – must be completed before a curative‑intent hepatectomy can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
 Continue systemic therapy with a regimen appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab or a second‑line oxaliplatin‑based doublet if not previously used).  
 Apply a liver‑directed local treatment to the progressing segment VII metastasis:  
  – Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) or microwave ablation if the lesion is amenable, or stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) if ablation is technically limited.  
 Re‑image the liver (triphasic CT or gadoxetate‑enhanced MRI) 6–8 weeks after the change in systemic therapy / ablative procedure to assess:  
  – Response of all remaining lesions (stable or regressed).  
  – Distribution of disease (unilobar vs. bilobar).  
  – FLR volume (CT‑volumetry).  
 If disease is now controlled (no progression) and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if prior extensive chemotherapy), proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection:  
  – Plan an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection that achieves R0 margins, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
  – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
 Sequence of primary tumor management:  
  – The left‑sided colon primary is asymptomatic; a liver‑first approach is reasonable to avoid delay of curative liver surgery.  
  – After hepatic resection and recovery, perform definitive colectomy (open or minimally invasive) with appropriate oncologic margins.  
 Post‑operative management:  
  – Resume adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (same regimen if tolerated) for 3–6 months to address micrometastatic disease.  
  – Surveillance with 3‑monthly imaging for the first year, then every 6 months, including CEA monitoring.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
 Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, ICG clearance).  
 Performance status / comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary reserve).  
 Exact anatomical distribution of the six stable lesions (segmental locations, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures).  
 Size of each stable lesion.  
 Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
 Details of the chemotherapy regimen already given (agents, number of cycles, response assessment per RECIST).  
 Whether the primary colon tumor has been resected or is symptomatic.  
 Baseline carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) trend.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability, select the optimal systemic regimen, and decide on the need for adjunctive liver‑directed therapies or hypertrophy procedures.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations diverge on several key aspects. 

1. **Completeness:** Recommendation 1 considers the disease potentially resectable, pending further control of the disease and confirmation of adequate FLR, while Recommendation 2 deems the situation currently unresectable, with a focus on systemic control and possible cytoreduction rather than aiming for complete R0 resection. Furthermore, Recommendation 1 provides a detailed outline of the surgical strategy, adjuvant therapy, and surveillance that is missing or differently emphasized in Recommendation 2.

2. **Step-by-step concordance:** The initial assessment of resectability differs, impacting subsequent steps. Recommendation 1 assumes potential resectability upon disease control, while Recommendation 2 suggests unresectability at present and focuses on cytoreduction. The management plans diverge significantly with differing strategic goals.

3. **Case-tailoring concordance:** Recommendation 1 includes specific management strategies based on KRAS mutation status and offers detailed surgical and systemic plans tailored to the case specifics, such as liver-first approach due to the asymptomatic primary tumor. Recommendation 2 mentions considering molecular profiles like MSS/MSI but does not tailor the systemic therapy decisions based on such profiles in as much detail as Recommendation 1.

4. **Missing data concordance:** Both recommendations identify the need for some similar missing data, such as FLR estimation and the status of extrahepatic disease. However, Recommendation 2 emphasizes precise anatomical mapping and molecular profiling considerations, including ctDNA and CTCs, which are not discussed in Recommendation 1, leading to discrepancies in identifying critical missing information.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  

 The liver metastases are radiologically absent after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but radiologic complete response does not guarantee eradication of microscopic disease (literature shows occult residual disease is common).  
 Technical feasibility of hepatic resection (or limited segmental resection/ablation of the original sites) cannot be confirmed without high‑resolution imaging (gadoxetate‑enhanced MRI or PET‑CT) and assessment of future liver remnant (FLR).  
 The primary rectal tumor has not been addressed surgically; its resectability (need for low‑anterior resection, possible sphincter‑preserving approach, need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy) is still unknown.  
 Because a specific prerequisite (advanced liver imaging and FLR assessment) is required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, the case falls into the “Potentially resectable” category.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Confirm disease status  
    Obtain gadoxetate‑enhanced liver MRI (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult hepatic disease and to map the prior metastatic sites.  
    Perform a high‑resolution pelvic MRI and/or endoscopic assessment to define the current extent of the rectal primary.  
    Calculate FLR using volumetric CT or MRI; ensure ≥30 % FLR (or >0.5 % body‑weight ratio).  

2. Multidisciplinary planning  
    Present imaging results at MDT (hepatic surgeon, colorectal surgeon, radiologist, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist).  
    Decide between a simultaneous versus staged approach:  
     – If the rectal primary is T3‑N1 and responsive, a simultaneous low‑anterior resection with liver exploration can be considered.  
     – If the primary requires further down‑staging (e.g., residual T3‑T4 disease), schedule a short‑course radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy first, then proceed to surgery.  

3. Surgical intervention  
    Liver – Perform intra‑operative ultrasound to locate any residual lesions.  
     – If no disease is visualised, a limited anatomical resection of the segments that previously harboured metastases (e.g., segmentectomy) can be performed to obtain negative margins, or the liver can be left untouched with only intra‑operative sampling of the prior sites.  
     – If residual lesions are identified, proceed with parenchymal‑sparing resection or ablation to achieve R0 resection while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
    Rectum – Execute a curative low‑anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving surgery) with total mesorectal excision. Consider a protective loop ileostomy if indicated.  

4. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
    Start adjuvant FOLFOX (or CAPOX) for 6 months, beginning within 6–8 weeks after surgery, to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
    Omit biologic agents in the adjuvant setting unless a trial or specific indication exists (evidence shows no OS benefit).  

5. Surveillance  
    Monitor CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
    Imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

 High‑resolution liver MRI (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult hepatic disease and to delineate prior metastatic sites.  
 Detailed staging of the rectal primary (MRI pelvis, endoscopic findings, current T/N stage).  
 Liver function tests and volumetric assessment to calculate future liver remnant.  
 Patient performance status (ECOG/ASA), comorbidities, and baseline hepatic reserve.  
 Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) to inform adjuvant decisions.  
 Information on whether any neoadjuvant radiotherapy has already been given to the rectum.  

These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
- Category: Resectable upfront  
- Reasoning:  
   Imaging shows a solitary 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, with no other intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease.  
   Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V has left sufficient hepatic parenchyma (segments I, II, III, VI, VIII) to preserve a future liver remnant (FLR) well above the 30 % threshold required for safe resection.  
   KRAS mutation is a negative prognostic factor but does not preclude curative surgery; it only influences systemic‑therapy choice.  
   No vascular invasion, biliary involvement, or need for complex reconstruction is reported.  
   Therefore, an R0 resection can be achieved immediately without prerequisite therapy or additional information.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up  
   Obtain liver volumetry (CT‑based) to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.5 % body‑weight ratio).  
   Review baseline labs (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assess performance status (ECOG 0‑1).  
   Confirm that the primary colorectal tumor has been resected with negative margins; if not, plan synchronous or staged colorectal resection according to symptom burden.  

- Surgical plan  
   Perform a formal anatomical segment VII resection (segmentectomy) or a non‑anatomical wedge excision with ≥ 1 cm macroscopic margin, aiming for R0 pathology.  
   Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
   Preserve inflow/outflow of the remaining segments; no need for portal vein embolisation or two‑stage hepatectomy given adequate FLR.
